Maximally localized Wannier functions: Theory and applications

Nicola Marzari Affiliation: Theory and Simulation of Materials (THEOS), École Polytechnique Fédérale de Lausanne, Station 12, 1015 Lausanne, Switzerland    Arash A. Mostofi Affiliation: Departments of Materials and Physics, and the Thomas Young Centre for Theory and Simulation of Materials, Imperial College London, London SW7 2AZ, UK    Jonathan R. Yates Affiliation: Department of Materials, University of Oxford, Parks Road, Oxford OX1 3PH, UK    Ivo Souza Affiliation: Centro de Física de Materiales (CSIC) and DIPC, Universidad del País Vasco, 20018 San Sebastián, Spain Affiliation: Ikerbasque, Basque Foundation for Science, 48011 Bilbao, Spain    David Vanderbilt Affiliation: Department of Physics and Astronomy, Rutgers University, Piscataway, NJ 08854-8019, USA
Abstract

The electronic ground state of a periodic system is usually described in terms of extended Bloch orbitals, but an alternative representation in terms of localized “Wannier functions” was introduced by Gregory Wannier in 1937. The connection between the Bloch and Wannier representations is realized by families of transformations in a continuous space of unitary matrices, carrying a large degree of arbitrariness. Since 1997, methods have been developed that allow one to iteratively transform the extended Bloch orbitals of a first-principles calculation into a unique set of maximally localized Wannier functions, accomplishing the solid-state equivalent of constructing localized molecular orbitals, or “Boys orbitals” as previously known from the chemistry literature. These developments are reviewed here, and a survey of the applications of these methods is presented. This latter includes a description of their use in analyzing the nature of chemical bonding, or as a local probe of phenomena related to electric polarization and orbital magnetization. Wannier interpolation schemes are also reviewed, by which quantities computed on a coarse reciprocal-space mesh can be used to interpolate onto much finer meshes at low cost, and applications in which Wannier functions are used as efficient basis functions are discussed. Finally the construction and use of Wannier functions outside the context of electronic-structure theory is presented, for cases that include phonon excitations, photonic crystals, and cold-atom optical lattices.

I INTRODUCTION

In the independent-particle approximation, the electronic ground state of a system is determined by specifying a set of one-particle orbitals and their occupations. For the case of periodic system, these one-particle orbitals are normally taken to be the Bloch functions ψn​𝐤​(𝐫)\psi_{n{\bf k}}({\bf r}) that are labeled, according to Bloch’s theorem, by a crystal momentum 𝐤\bf k lying inside the Brillouin zone and a band index nn. Although this choice is by far the most widely used in electronic-structure calculations, alternative representations are possible. In particular, to arrive at the Wannier representation [491, 212, 79], one carries out a unitary transformation from the Bloch functions to a set of localized “Wannier functions” (WFs) labeled by a cell index 𝐑\bf R and a band-like index nn, such that in a crystal the WFs at different 𝐑\bf R are translational images of one another. Unlike Bloch functions, WFs are not eigenstates of the Hamiltonian; in selecting them, one trades off localization in energy for localization in space.

In the earlier solid-state theory literature, WFs were typically introduced in order to carry out some formal derivation – for example, of the effective-mass treatment of electron dynamics, or of an effective spin Hamiltonian – but actual calculations of the WFs were rarely performed. The history is rather different in the chemistry literature, where “localized molecular orbitals” (LMO’s) [54, 131, 132, 104, 55] have played a significant role in computational chemistry since its early days. Chemists have emphasized that such a representation can provide an insightful picture of the nature of the chemical bond in a material — otherwise missing from the picture of extended eigenstates — or can serve as a compact basis set for high-accuracy calculations.

The actual implementation of Wannier’s vision in the context of first-principles electronic-structure calculations, such as those carried out in the Kohn-Sham framework of density-functional theory [216], has instead been slower to unfold. A major reason for this is that WFs are strongly non-unique. This is a consequence of the phase indeterminacy that Bloch orbitals ψn​𝐤\psi_{n{\bf k}} have at every wavevector k – or, more generally, the “gauge” indeterminacy associated with the freedom to apply any arbitrary unitary transformation to the occupied Bloch states at each 𝐤{\bf k}. This second indeterminacy is all the more troublesome in the common case of degeneracy for the occupied bands at certain high-symmetry points in the Brillouin zone, making a partition into separate “bands”, that could separately be transformed in Wannier functions, problematic. Therefore, even before one could attempt to compute the WFs for a given material, one had first to resolve the question of which states to use to compute WFs.

An important development in this regard was the introduction by Marzari and Vanderbilt [273] of a “maximal localization” criterion for identifying a unique set of WFs for a given crystalline insulator. The approach is similar in spirit to the construction of LMO’s in chemistry, but its implementation in the solid-state context required significant developments, due to the ill-conditioned nature of the position operator in periodic systems [303], that was clarified in the context of the “modern theory” of polarization [206, 356]. Marzari and Vanderbilt showed that the minimization of a localization functional corresponding to the sum of the second-moment spread of each Wannier charge density about its own center of charge was both formally attractive and computationally tractable. In a related development, Souza et al. [426] generalized the method to handle the case in which one wants to construct a set of WFs that spans a subspace containing, e.g., the partially occupied bands of a metal.

These developments touched off a transformational shift in which the computational electronic-structure community started constructing maximally-localized WFs (MLWFs) explicitly and using these for different purposes. The reasons are manifold: First, WFs, akin to LMO’s in molecules, provide an insightful chemical analysis of the nature of bonding, and its evolution during, say, a chemical reaction. As such, they have become an established tool in the post-processing of electronic-structure calculations. More interestingly, there are formal connections between the centers of charge of the WFs and the Berry phases of the Bloch functions as they are carried around the Brillouin zone. This connection is embodied in the microscopic modern theory of polarization, alluded to above, and has led to important advances in the characterization and understanding of dielectric response and polarization in materials. Of broader interest to the entire condensed matter community is the use of WFs in the construction of model Hamiltonians for, e.g., correlated-electron and magnetic systems. An alternative use of WFs as localized, transferable building blocks has taken place in the theory of ballistic (Landauer) transport, where Green’s functions and self-energies can be constructed effectively in a Wannier basis, or that of first-principles tight-binding Hamiltonians, where chemically-accurate Hamiltonians are constructed directly on the Wannier basis, rather than fitted or inferred from macroscopic considerations. Finally, the ideas that were developed for electronic WFs have also seen application in very different contexts. For example, MLWF’s have been used in the theoretical analysis of phonons, photonic crystals, cold atom lattices, and the local dielectric responses of insulators.

Here we review these developments. We first introduce the transformation from Bloch functions to WFs in Sec. II, discussing their gauge freedom and the methods developed for constructing WFs through projection or maximal localization. A “disentangling procedure” for constructing WFs for a non-isolated set of bands (e.g., in metals) is also described. In Sec. III we discuss variants of these procedures in which different localization criteria or different algorithms are used, and discuss the relationship to “downfolding” and linear-scaling methods. Sec. IV describes how the calculation of WFs has proved to be a useful tool for analyzing the nature of the chemical bonding in crystalline, amorphous, and defective systems. Of particular importance is the ability to use WFs as a local probe of electric polarization, as described in Sec. V. There we also discuss how the Wannier representation has been useful in describing orbital magnetization, NMR chemical shifts, orbital magnetoelectric responses, and topological insulators. Sec. VI describes Wannier interpolation schemes, by which quantities computed on a relatively coarse 𝐤{\bf k}-space mesh can be used to interpolate faithfully onto an arbitrarily fine 𝐤{\bf k}-space mesh at relatively low cost. In Sec. VII we discuss applications in which the WFs are used as an efficient basis for the calculations of quantum transport properties, the derivation of semiempirical potentials, and for describing strongly-correlated systems. Sec. VIII contains a brief discussion of the construction and use of WFs in contexts other than electronic-structure theory, including for phonons in ordinary crystals, photonic crystals, and cold atoms in optical lattices. Finally, Sec. IX provides a short summary and conclusions.

II REVIEW OF BASIC THEORY

II.1 Bloch functions and Wannier functions

Electronic structure calculations are often carried out using periodic boundary conditions. This is the most natural choice for the study of perfect crystals, and also applies to the common use of periodic supercells for the study of non-periodic systems such as liquids, interfaces, and defects. The one-particle effective Hamiltonian HH then commutes with the lattice-translation operator T𝐑{T}_{\bf R}, allowing one to choose as common eigenstates the Bloch orbitals |ψn​𝐤⟩|\,\psi_{n{\bf k}}\,\rangle:

[H,T𝐑]= 0⇒ψn​𝐤​(𝐫)=un​𝐤​(𝐫)​ei​𝐤⋅𝐫,[\,{H},\,{T}_{\bf R}\,]\;=\;0\;\;\Rightarrow\;\;\psi_{n{\bf k}}({\bf r})\;=\;u_{n{\bf k}}({\bf r})\,e^{i{\bf k\cdot r}}\;\;, (1)

where un​𝐤​(𝐫)u_{n{\bf k}}({\bf r}) has the periodicity of the Hamiltonian.

Several Bloch functions are sketched on the left-hand side of Fig. 1 for a toy model in which the band of interest is composed of pp-like orbitals centered on each atom. For the moment, we suppose that this band is an isolated band, i.e., it remains separated by a gap from the bands below and above at all 𝐤{\bf k}. Since Bloch functions at different 𝐤{\bf k} have different envelope functions ei​𝐤⋅𝐫e^{i{\bf k}\cdot{\bf r}}, one can expect to be able to build a localized “wave packet” by superposing Bloch functions of different 𝐤{\bf k}. To get a very localized wave packet in real space, we need to use a very broad superposition in 𝐤{\bf k} space. But 𝐤{\bf k} lives in the periodic Brillouin zone, so the best we can do is to choose equal amplitudes all across the Brillouin zone. Thus, we can construct

w0​(𝐫)=V(2​π)3​∫BZd​𝐤​ψn​𝐤​(𝐫),w_{0}({\bf r})\;=\;\frac{V}{(2\pi)^{3}}\int_{\rm BZ}d{\bf k}\;\psi_{n{\bf k}}({\bf r})\ \;\;, (2)

where VV is the real-space primitive cell volume and the integral is carried over the Brillouin zone (BZ). (See Sec. II.1.3 for normalization conventions.) Equation (2) can be interpreted as the WF located in the home unit cell, as sketched in the top-right panel of Fig. 1.

More generally, we can insert a phase factor e−i𝐤⋅𝐑e^{-i{\bf k}\cdot{\bf R}} into the integrand of Eq. (2), where 𝐑{\bf R} is a real-space lattice vector; this has the effect of translating the real-space WF by 𝐑{\bf R}, generating additional WFs such as w1w_{1} and w2w_{2} sketched in Fig. 1. Switching to the Dirac bra-ket notation and introducing the notation that 𝐑​n{\bf R}n refers to the WF wn​𝐑w_{n{\bf R}} in cell 𝐑{\bf R} associated with band nn, WFs can be constructed according to [491]

|𝐑n⟩=V(2​π)3∫BZd𝐤e−i𝐤⋅𝐑|ψn​𝐤⟩.|{{\bf R}n}\rangle\;=\;\frac{V}{(2\pi)^{3}}\int_{\rm BZ}d{\bf k}\;e^{-i{\bf k\cdot{\bf R}}}\,|{\,\psi_{n{\bf k}}\,}\rangle\;\;. (3)

It is easily shown that the |𝐑​n⟩|\,{{\bf R}n}\,\rangle form an orthonormal set (see Sec. II.1.3) and that two WFs |𝐑​n⟩|\,{{\bf R}n}\,\rangle and |𝐑′​n⟩|\,{{\bf R}^{\prime}}n\,\rangle transform into each other under translation by the lattice vector 𝐑−𝐑′{\bf R}-{\bf R^{\prime}} [42]. Eq. (3) takes the form of a Fourier transform, and its inverse transform is

|ψn​𝐤⟩=∑𝐑ei​𝐤⋅𝐑​|𝐑​n⟩|{\,\psi_{n{\bf k}}\,}\rangle\;=\;\sum_{\bf R}\,e^{i{\bf k}\cdot{\bf R}}\,|{{\bf R}n}\rangle (4)

(see Sec. II.1.3). Any of the Bloch functions on the left side of Fig. 1 can thus be built up by linearly superposing the WFs shown on the right side, when the appropriate phases ei​𝐤⋅𝐑e^{i{\bf k}\cdot{\bf R}} are used.

The transformations of Eqs. (3) and (4) constitute a unitary transformation between Bloch and Wannier states. Thus, both sets of states provide an equally valid description of the band subspace, even if the WFs are not Hamiltonian eigenstates. For example, the charge density obtained by summing the squares of the Bloch functions |ψn​𝐤⟩|{\psi_{n{\bf k}}}\rangle or the WFs |𝐑​n⟩|{{\bf R}n}\rangle is identical; a similar reasoning applies to the trace of any one-particle operator. The equivalence between the Bloch and the Wannier representations can also be made manifest by expressing the band projection operator P{P} in both representations, i.e., as

P=V(2​π)3​∫BZd​𝐤​|ψn​𝐤⟩​⟨ψn​𝐤|=∑𝐑|𝐑​n⟩​⟨𝐑​n|.{P}=\frac{V}{(2\pi)^{3}}\int_{\rm BZ}d{\bf k}\;|{\psi_{n{\bf k}}}\rangle\langle\psi_{n{\bf k}}|=\sum_{\bf R}|{{\bf R}n}\rangle\langle{\bf R}n|\;. (5)

WFs thus provide an attractive option for representing the space spanned by a Bloch band in a crystal, being localized while still carrying the same information contained in the Bloch functions.

II.1.1 Gauge freedom

However, the theory of WFs is made more complex by the presence of a “gauge freedom” that exists in the definition of the ψn​𝐤\psi_{n{\bf k}}. In fact, we can replace

|ψ~n​𝐤⟩=ei​φn​(𝐤)​|ψn​𝐤⟩,|\,\tilde{\psi}_{n{\bf k}}\,\rangle\;=\;e^{i\varphi_{n}({\bf k})}\,|\,\psi_{n{\bf k}}\,\rangle\;\;, (6)

or equivalently,

|u~n​𝐤⟩=ei​φn​(𝐤)​|un​𝐤⟩,|\,\tilde{u}_{n{\bf k}}\,\rangle\;=\;e^{i\varphi_{n}({\bf k})}\,|\,u_{n{\bf k}}\,\rangle\;\;, (7)

without changing the physical description of the system, with φn​(𝐤)\varphi_{n}({\bf k}) being any real function that is periodic in reciprocal space.11 1 More precisely, the condition is that φn​(𝐤+𝐆)=φn​(𝐤)+𝐆⋅Δ​𝐑\varphi_{n}({\bf k}+{\bf G})=\varphi_{n}({\bf k})+{\bf G}\cdot\Delta{\bf R} for any reciprocal-lattice translation 𝐆{\bf G}, where Δ​𝐑\Delta{\bf R} is a real-space lattice vector. This allows for the possibility that φn\varphi_{n} may shift by 2​π2\pi times an integer upon translation by 𝐆\bf G; the vector Δ​𝐑\Delta{\bf R} expresses the corresponding shift in the position of the resulting WF. A smooth gauge could, e.g., be defined such that ∇𝐤|un​𝐤⟩\nabla_{\bf k}|u_{n{\bf k}}\rangle is well defined at all 𝐤\bf k. Henceforth we shall assume that the Bloch functions on the right-hand side of Eq. (3) belong to a smooth gauge, since we would not get well-localized WFs on the left-hand side otherwise. This is typical of Fourier transforms: the smoother the reciprocal-space object, the more localized the resulting real-space object, and vice versa.

One way to see this explicitly is to consider the 𝐑=0{\bf R}=0 home-cell wn​0​(𝐫)w_{n0}({\bf r}) evaluated at a distant point 𝐫{\bf r}; using Eq. (1) in Eq. (3), this is given by ∫BZun​𝐤​(𝐫)​ei​𝐤⋅𝐫​𝑑𝐤\int_{\rm BZ}\,\,u_{n{\bf k}}({\bf r})e^{i{\bf k}\cdot{\bf r}}\,d{\bf k}, which will be small due to cancellations arising from the rapid variation of the exponential factor, provided that un​𝐤u_{n{\bf k}} is a smooth function of 𝐤{\bf k} [42].

It is important to realize that the gauge freedom of Eqs. (6) and (7) propagates into the WFs. That is, different choices of smooth gauge correspond to different sets of WFs having in general different shapes and spreads. In this sense, the WFs are “more non-unique” than the Bloch functions, which only acquire a phase change. We also emphasize that there is no “preferred gauge” assigned by the Schrödinger equation to the Bloch orbitals. Thus, the non-uniqueness of the WFs resulting from Eq. (3) is unavoidable.

II.1.2 Multiband case

Before discussing how this non-uniqueness might be resolved, we first relax the condition that band nn be a single isolated band, and consider instead a manifold of JJ bands that remain separated with respect to any lower or higher bands outside the manifold. Internal degeneracies and crossings among the JJ bands may occur in general. In the simplest case this manifold corresponds to the occupied bands of an insulator, but more generally it consists of any set of bands that is separated by a gap from both lower and higher bands everywhere in the Brillouin zone. Traces over this band manifold are invariant with respect to any unitary transformation among the JJ occupied Bloch orbitals at a given wavevector, so it is natural to generalize the notion of a “gauge transformation” to

|ψ~n​𝐤⟩=∑m=1JUm​n(𝐤)​|ψm​𝐤⟩.|\,\tilde{\psi}_{n{\bf k}}\,\rangle=\sum_{m=1}^{J}\,U_{mn}^{({\bf k})}\,|\,\psi_{m{\bf k}}\,\rangle\;\;. (8)

Here Um​n(𝐤)U_{mn}^{({\bf k})} is a unitary matrix of dimension JJ that is periodic in 𝐤\bf k, with Eq. (6) corresponding to the special case of a diagonal UU matrix. It follows that the projection operator onto this band manifold at wavevector 𝐤{\bf k},

P𝐤=∑n=1J|ψn​𝐤⟩​⟨ψn​𝐤|=∑n=1J|ψ~n​𝐤⟩​⟨ψ~n​𝐤|{P}_{\,{\bf k}}=\sum_{n=1}^{J}|{\psi_{n{\bf k}}}\rangle\langle\psi_{n{\bf k}}|=\sum_{n=1}^{J}|{\tilde{\psi}_{n{\bf k}}}\rangle\langle\tilde{\psi}_{n{\bf k}}| (9)

is invariant, even though the |ψ~n​𝐤⟩|\tilde{\psi}_{n{\bf k}}\rangle resulting from Eq. (8) are no longer generally eigenstates of H{H}, and nn is no longer a band index in the usual sense.

Our goal is again to construct WFs out of these transformed Bloch functions using Eq. (3). Figs. 2(a) and (b) show, for example, what the result might eventually look like for the case of the four occupied valence bands of Si or GaAs, respectively. From these four bands, one obtains four equivalent WFs per unit cell, each localized on one of the four nearest-neighbor Si-Si or Ga-As bonds. The presence of a bond-centered inversion symmetry for Si, but not GaAs, is clearly reflected in the shapes of the WFs.

Once again, we emphasize that the gauge freedom expressed in Eq. (8) implies that the WFs are strongly non-unique. This is illustrated in Fig. 3, which shows an alternative construction of WFs for GaAs. The WF on the left was constructed from the lowest valence band nn=1, while the one on the right is one of three constructed from bands nn=2-4. The former has primarily As ss character and the latter has primarily As pp character, although both (and especially the latter) contain some Ga ss and pp character as well. The WFs of Figs. 2(b) and Fig. 3 are related to each other by a certain manifold of 4×\times4 unitary matrices Un​m(𝐤)U_{nm}^{({\bf k})} relating their Bloch transforms in the manner of Eq. (8).

However, before we can arrive at well-localized WFs like those shown in Figs. 2 and 3, we again have to address questions of smoothness of the gauge choice expressed in Eq. (8). This issue is even more profound in the present multiband case, since this smoothness criterion is generally incompatible with the usual construction of Bloch functions. That is, if we simply insert the usual Bloch functions |ψn​𝐤⟩|{\psi_{n{\bf k}}}\rangle, defined to be eigenstates of H{H}, into the right-hand side of Eq. (3), it is generally not possible to produce well-localized WFs. The problem arises when there are degeneracies among the bands in question at certain locations in the Brillouin zone. Consider, for example, what happens if we try to construct a single WF from the highest occupied band n=4n=4 in GaAs. This would be doomed to failure, since this band becomes degenerate with bands two and three at the zone center, Γ\Gamma, as shown in Fig. 3. As a result, band four is non-analytic in 𝐤{\bf k} in the vicinity of Γ\Gamma. The Fourier transform of Eq. (3) would then result in a poorly localized object having power-law tails in real space.

In such cases, therefore, the extra unitary mixing expressed in Eq. (8) is mandatory, even if it may be optional in the case of a set of discrete bands that do not touch anywhere in the BZ. So, generally speaking, our procedure must be that we start from a set of Hamiltonian eigenstates |ψn​𝐤⟩|{\psi_{n{\bf k}}}\rangle that are not per se smooth in 𝐤{\bf k}, and introduce unitary rotations Um​n(𝐤)U_{mn}^{({\bf k})} that “cancel out” the discontinuities in such a way that smoothness is restored, i.e., that the resulting |ψ~n​𝐤⟩|{\tilde{\psi}_{n{\bf k}}}\rangle of Eq. (8) obey the smoothness condition that ∇𝐤|ψ~n​𝐤⟩\nabla_{\bf k}|{\tilde{\psi}_{n{\bf k}}}\rangle remains regular at all 𝐤{\bf k}. Then, when these |ψ~n​𝐤⟩|{\tilde{\psi}_{n{\bf k}}}\rangle are inserted into Eq. (3) in place of the |ψn​𝐤⟩|{\psi_{n{\bf k}}}\rangle, well-localized WFs should result. Explicitly, this results in WFs constructed according to

|𝐑n⟩=V(2​π)3∫BZd𝐤e−i𝐤⋅𝐑∑m=1JUm​n(𝐤)|ψm​𝐤⟩.|\,{{\bf R}n}\,\rangle\;=\;\frac{V}{(2\pi)^{3}}\int_{\rm BZ}d{\bf k}\,e^{-i{\bf k\cdot{\bf R}}}\,\sum_{m=1}^{J}\,U_{mn}^{({\bf k})}\,|\,\psi_{m{\bf k}}\,\rangle\;\;. (10)

The question remains how to choose the unitary rotations Um​n(𝐤)U_{mn}^{({\bf k})} so as to accomplish this task. We will see that one way to do this is to use a projection technique, as outlined in the next section. Ideally, however, we would like the construction to result in WFs that are “maximally localized” according to some criterion. Methods for accomplishing this are discussed in Sec. II.3

II.1.3 Normalization conventions

In the above equations, formulated for continuous 𝐤{\bf k}, we have adopted the convention that Bloch functions are normalized to one unit cell, ∫Vd​𝐫​|ψn​𝐤​(𝐫)|2=1\int_{V}d{\bf r}\,|\psi_{n{\bf k}}({\bf r})|^{2}=1, even though they extend over the entire crystal. We also define ⟨f|g⟩\langle f|{g}\rangle as the integral of f∗​gf^{*}g over all space. With this notation, ⟨ψn​𝐤|ψn​𝐤⟩\langle\psi_{n{\bf k}}|{\psi_{n{\bf k}}}\rangle is not unity; instead, it diverges according to the rule

⟨ψn​𝐤|ψm​𝐤′⟩=(2​π)3V​δn​m​δ3​(𝐤−𝐤′).\langle\psi_{n{\bf k}}|{\psi_{m{\bf k}^{\prime}}}\rangle=\frac{(2\pi)^{3}}{V}\,\delta_{nm}\,\delta^{3}({\bf k}-{\bf k}^{\prime})\;\;. (11)

With these conventions it is easy to check that the WFs in Eqs. (3-4) are properly normalized, i.e., ⟨𝐑​n|𝐑′​m⟩=δ𝐑𝐑′​δn​m\langle{\bf R}n|{{\bf R}^{\prime}m}\rangle=\delta_{{\bf R}{\bf R}^{\prime}}\,\delta_{nm}.

It is often more convenient to work on a discrete uniform 𝐤{\bf k} mesh instead of continuous 𝐤{\bf k} space.22 2 The discretization of 𝐤{\bf k}-space amounts to imposing periodic boundary conditions on the Bloch wavefunctions over a supercell in real space. Thus, it should be kept in mind that the WFs given by Eqs. (12) and (14) are not truly localized, as they also display the supercell periodicity (and are normalized to a supercell volume). Under these circumstances the notion of “Wannier localization” refers to localization within one supercell, which is meaningful for supercells chosen large enough to ensure negligible overlap between a WF and its periodic images. Letting NN be the number of unit cells in the periodic supercell, or equivalently, the number of mesh points in the BZ, it is possible to keep the conventions close to the continuous case by defining the Fourier transform pair as

|ψn​𝐤⟩\displaystyle|{\psi_{n{\bf k}}}\rangle =\displaystyle= ∑𝐑ei​𝐤⋅𝐑​|𝐑​n⟩\displaystyle\sum_{\bf R}\,e^{i{\bf k}\cdot{\bf R}}\,|{{\bf R}n}\rangle\; (12)
⇕\displaystyle\Updownarrow
|𝐑​n⟩\displaystyle|{{\bf R}n}\rangle =\displaystyle= 1N∑𝐤e−i𝐤⋅𝐑|ψn​𝐤⟩\displaystyle\frac{1}{N}\sum_{\bf k}\,e^{-i{\bf k}\cdot{\bf R}}\,|{\psi_{n{\bf k}}}\rangle

with ⟨ψn​𝐤|ψm​𝐤′⟩=N​δn​m​δ𝐤𝐤′\langle\psi_{n{\bf k}}|{\psi_{m{\bf k}^{\prime}}}\rangle=N\delta_{nm}\,\delta_{{\bf k}{\bf k}^{\prime}}, so that Eq. (5) becomes, after generalizing to the multiband case,

P=1N​∑n​𝐤|ψn​𝐤⟩​⟨ψn​𝐤|=∑n​𝐑|𝐑​n⟩​⟨𝐑​n|.{P}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{n{\bf k}}|{\psi_{n{\bf k}}}\rangle\langle\psi_{n{\bf k}}|=\sum_{n{\bf R}}|{{\bf R}n}\rangle\langle{\bf R}n|\;. (13)

Another commonly used convention is to write

|ψn​𝐤⟩\displaystyle|{\psi_{n{\bf k}}}\rangle =\displaystyle= 1N​∑𝐑ei​𝐤⋅𝐑​|𝐑​n⟩\displaystyle\frac{1}{\sqrt{N}}\sum_{\bf R}\,e^{i{\bf k}\cdot{\bf R}}\,|{{\bf R}n}\rangle\; (14)
⇕\displaystyle\Updownarrow
|𝐑​n⟩\displaystyle|{{\bf R}n}\rangle =\displaystyle= 1N∑𝐤e−i𝐤⋅𝐑|ψn​𝐤⟩\displaystyle\frac{1}{\sqrt{N}}\sum_{\bf k}\,e^{-i{\bf k}\cdot{\bf R}}\,|{\psi_{n{\bf k}}}\rangle

with ⟨ψn​𝐤|ψm​𝐤′⟩=δn​m​δ𝐤𝐤′\langle\psi_{n{\bf k}}|{\psi_{m{\bf k}^{\prime}}}\rangle=\delta_{nm}\,\delta_{{\bf k}{\bf k}^{\prime}} and Eq. (13) replaced by

P=∑n​𝐤|ψn​𝐤⟩​⟨ψn​𝐤|=∑n​𝐑|𝐑​n⟩​⟨𝐑​n|.{P}=\sum_{n{\bf k}}|{\psi_{n{\bf k}}}\rangle\langle\psi_{n{\bf k}}|=\sum_{n{\bf R}}|{{\bf R}n}\rangle\langle{\bf R}n|\;. (15)

In either case, it is convenient to keep the |un​𝐤⟩|{u_{n{\bf k}}}\rangle functions normalized to the unit cell, with inner products involving them, such as ⟨um​𝐤|un​𝐤⟩\langle u_{m{\bf k}}|{u_{n{\bf k}}}\rangle, understood as integrals over one unit cell. In the case of Eq. (14), this means that un​𝐤(𝐫)=Ne−i𝐤⋅𝐫ψn​𝐤(𝐫)u_{n{\bf k}}({\bf r})=\sqrt{N}e^{-i{\bf k}\cdot{\bf r}}\psi_{n{\bf k}}({\bf r}).

II.2 Wannier functions via projection

A simple yet often effective approach for constructing a smooth gauge in 𝐤{\bf k}, and a corresponding set of well-localized WFs, is by projection - an approach that finds its roots in the analysis of des Cloizeaux [80]. Here, as discussed, e.g., in Sec. IV.G.1 of Marzari and Vanderbilt [273], one starts from a set of JJ localized trial orbitals gn​(𝐫)g_{n}(\bf r) corresponding to some rough guess for the WFs in the home unit cell. Returning to the continuous-𝐤{\bf k} formulation, these gn​(𝐫)g_{n}(\bf r) are projected onto the Bloch manifold at wavevector 𝐤\bf k to obtain

|ϕn​𝐤⟩=∑m=1J|ψm​𝐤⟩​⟨ψm​𝐤|gn⟩,|\phi_{n\bf k}\rangle=\sum_{m=1}^{J}\,|\psi_{m\bf k}\rangle\langle\psi_{m\bf k}|g_{n}\rangle\;, (16)

which are typically smooth in 𝐤{\bf k}-space, albeit not orthonormal. (The integral in ⟨ψm​𝐤|gn⟩\langle\psi_{m\bf k}|g_{n}\rangle is over all space as usual.) We note that in actual practice such projection is achieved by first computing a matrix of inner products (A𝐤)m​n=⟨ψm​𝐤|gn⟩(A_{\bf k})_{mn}=\langle\psi_{m\bf k}|g_{n}\rangle and then using these in Eq. (16). The overlap matrix (S𝐤)m​n=⟨ϕm​𝐤|ϕn​𝐤⟩V=(A𝐤†​A𝐤)m​n(S_{\bf k})_{mn}=\langle\phi_{m\bf k}|\phi_{n\bf k}\rangle_{V}=(A_{\bf k}^{\dagger}A_{\bf k}^{\phantom{\dagger}})_{mn} (where subscript VV denotes an integral over one cell) is then computed and used to construct the Löwdin-orthonormalized Bloch-like states

|ψ~n​𝐤⟩=∑m=1J|ϕm​𝐤⟩(S𝐤−1/2)m​n.|\tilde{\psi}_{n\bf k}\rangle=\sum_{m=1}^{J}\,|\phi_{m\bf k}\rangle(S_{\bf k}^{-1/2})_{mn}\;. (17)

These |ψ~n​𝐤⟩|\tilde{\psi}_{n\bf k}\rangle have now a smooth gauge in 𝐤{\bf k}, are related to the original |ψn​𝐤⟩|\psi_{n\bf k}\rangle by a unitary transformation,33 3 One can prove that this transformation is unitary by performing the singular value decomposition A=Z​D​W†A=ZDW^{\dagger}, with ZZ and WW unitary and DD real and diagonal. It follows that A(A†A)−1/2A(A^{\dagger}A)^{-1/2} is equal to Z​W†ZW^{\dagger}, and thus unitary. and when substituted into Eq. (3) in place of the |ψn​𝐤⟩|\psi_{n{\bf k}}\rangle result in a set of well-localized WFs. We note in passing that the |ψ~n​𝐤⟩|\tilde{\psi}_{n\bf k}\rangle are uniquely defined by the trial orbitals gn​(𝐫)g_{n}(\bf r) and the chosen (isolated) manifold, since any arbitrary unitary rotation among the |ψn​𝐤⟩|\psi_{n\bf k}\rangle orbitals cancels out exactly and does not affect the outcome of Eq. 16, eliminating thus any gauge freedom.

We emphasize that the trial functions do not need to resemble the target WFs closely; it is often sufficient to choose simple analytic functions (e.g., spherical harmonics times Gaussians) provided they are roughly located on sites where WFs are expected to be centered and have appropriate angular character. The method is successful as long as the inner-product matrix A𝐤A_{\bf k} does not become singular (or nearly so) for any 𝐤{\bf k}, which can be ensured by checking that the ratio of maximum and minimum values of detS𝐤\det S_{\bf k} in the Brillouin zone does not become too large. For example, spherical (ss-like) Gaussians located at the bond centers will suffice for the construction of well-localized WFs, akin to those shown in Fig. 2, spanning the four occupied valence bands of semiconductors such as Si and GaAs.

II.3 Maximally localized Wannier functions

The projection method described in the previous subsection has been used by many authors [441, 228, 263, 348], as has a related method involving downfolding of the band structure onto a minimal basis [10, 522]; some of these approaches will also be discussed in Sec. III.2. Other authors have made use of symmetry considerations, analyticity requirements, and variational procedures [431, 432, 418]. A very general and now widely used approach, however, has been that developed by Marzari and Vanderbilt [273] in which localization is enforced by introducing a well-defined localization criterion, and then refining the Um​n(𝐤)U_{mn}^{({\bf k})} in order to satisfy that criterion. We first give an overview of this approach, and then provide details in the following subsections.

First, the localization functional

Ω\displaystyle\Omega =\displaystyle= ∑n[⟨ 0​n|r2| 0​n⟩−⟨ 0​n|𝐫| 0​n⟩2]\displaystyle\sum_{n}\left[\langle\,{{\bf 0}n}\,|\,r^{2}\,|\,{{\bf 0}n}\,\rangle\,-\,\langle\,{{\bf 0}n}\,|\,{\bf r}\,|\,{{\bf 0}n}\,\rangle^{2}\,\right] (18)
=\displaystyle= ∑n[⟨r2⟩n−𝐫¯n2]\displaystyle\sum_{n}\left[\langle r^{2}\rangle_{n}-\bar{\bf r}_{n}^{2}\right]

is defined, measuring of the sum of the quadratic spreads of the JJ WFs in the home unit cell around their centers. This turns out to be the solid-state equivalent of the Foster-Boys criterion of quantum chemistry [54, 131, 132, 55]. The next step is to express Ω\Omega in terms of the Bloch functions. This requires some care, since expectation values of the position operator are not well defined in the Bloch representation. The needed formalism will be discussed briefly in Sec. II.3.1 and more extensively in Sec. V.1.1, with much of the conceptual work stemming from the earlier development the modern theory of polarization [42, 355, 206, 481, 356].

Once a 𝐤{\bf k}-space expression for Ω\Omega has been derived, maximally localized WFs are obtained by minimizing it with respect to the Um​n(𝐤)U_{mn}^{({\bf k})} appearing in Eq. (10). This is done as a post-processing step after a conventional electronic-structure calculation has been self-consistently converged and a set of ground-state Bloch orbitals |ψm​𝐤⟩|\,\psi_{m{\bf k}}\,\rangle has been chosen once and for all. The Um​n(𝐤)U_{mn}^{({\bf k})} are then iteratively refined in a direct minimization procedure of the localization functional that is outlined in Sec. II.4 below. This procedure also provides the expectation values ⟨r2⟩n\langle r^{2}\rangle_{n} and 𝐫¯n\bar{\bf r}_{n}; the latter, in particular, are the primary quantities needed to compute many of the properties, such as the electronic polarization, discussed in Sec. V. If desired, the resulting Um​n(𝐤)U_{mn}^{({\bf k})} can also be used to construct explicitly the maximally localized WFs via Eq. (10). This step is typically only necessary, however, if one wants to visualize the resulting WFs or to use them as basis functions for some subsequent analysis.

II.3.1 Real-space representation

An interesting consequence stemming from the choice of (18) as the localization functional is that it allows a natural decomposition of the functional into gauge-invariant and gauge-dependent parts. That is, we can write

Ω=ΩI+Ω~\Omega\,=\,\Omega_{\rm\,I}\,+\,\widetilde{\Omega} (19)

where

ΩI=∑n[⟨ 0​n|r2| 0​n⟩−∑𝐑​m|⟨𝐑​m​|𝐫|​𝟎​n⟩|2]\Omega_{\rm\,I}=\sum_{n}\left[\langle\,{{\bf 0}n}\,|\,r^{2}\,|\,{{\bf 0}n}\,\rangle\,-\,\sum_{{\bf R}m}\,\bigl|\langle{{\bf R}m}|{\bf r}|{\bf 0}n\rangle\bigr|^{2}\right] (20)

and

Ω~=∑n∑𝐑​m≠𝟎​n|⟨𝐑​m​|𝐫|​𝟎​n⟩|2.\widetilde{\Omega}=\sum_{n}\sum_{{\bf R}m\neq{\bf 0}n}\bigl|\langle{{\bf R}m}|{\bf r}|{\bf 0}n\rangle\bigr|^{2}\,. (21)

It can be shown that not only Ω~\widetilde{\Omega} but also ΩI\Omega_{\rm\,I} is positive definite, and moreover that ΩI\Omega_{\rm\,I} is gauge-invariant, i.e., invariant under any arbitrary unitary transformation (10) of the Bloch orbitals [273]. This follows straightforwardly from recasting Eq. (20) in terms of the band-group projection operator PP, as defined in Eq. (15), and its complement Q=1−PQ=1-P:

ΩI\displaystyle\Omega_{\rm\,I} =\displaystyle= ∑n​α⟨𝟎​n|rα​Q​rα|𝟎​n⟩\displaystyle\sum_{n\alpha}\langle{{\bf 0}n}|r_{\alpha}Qr_{\alpha}|{\bf 0}n\rangle (22)
=\displaystyle= ∑αTrc​[P​rα​Q​rα].\displaystyle\sum_{\alpha}{\rm Tr}_{\rm c}\,[Pr_{\alpha}Qr_{\alpha}]\;.

The subscript ‘c’ indicates trace per unit cell. Clearly ΩI\Omega_{\rm\,I} is gauge invariant, since it is expressed in terms of projection operators that are unaffected by any gauge transformation. It can also be seen to be positive definite by using the idempotency of PP and QQ to write ΩI=∑αTrc​[(P​rα​Q)​(P​rα​Q)†]=∑α‖P​rα​Q‖c2\Omega_{\rm\,I}=\sum_{\alpha}{\rm Tr}_{\rm c}\,[(Pr_{\alpha}Q)(Pr_{\alpha}Q)^{\dagger}]=\sum_{\alpha}||Pr_{\alpha}Q||_{\rm c}^{2}.

The minimization procedure of Ω\Omega thus actually corresponds to the minimization of the non-invariant part Ω~\widetilde{\Omega} only. At the minimum, the off-diagonal elements |⟨𝐑​m​|𝐫|​𝟎​n⟩|2\left|\langle{{\bf R}m}|{\bf r}|{\bf 0}n\rangle\right|^{2} are as small as possible, realizing the best compromise in the simultaneous diagonalization, within the subspace of the Bloch bands considered, of the three position operators xx, yy and zz, which do not in general commute when projected onto this space.

II.3.2 Reciprocal-space representation

As shown by Blount [42], matrix elements of the position operator between WFs take the form

⟨𝐑​n​|𝐫|​𝟎​m⟩=i​V(2​π)3​∫d​𝐤​ei​𝐤⋅𝐑​⟨un​𝐤|∇𝐤|um​𝐤⟩\langle{\bf R}n|{\bf r}|{\bf 0}m\rangle=i\,{\frac{V}{(2\pi)^{3}}}\int d{\bf k}\,e^{i{\bf k}\cdot{\bf R}}\langle u_{n{\bf k}}|\nabla_{\bf k}|u_{m{\bf k}}\rangle (23)

and

⟨𝐑n|r2|𝟎m⟩=−V(2​π)3∫d𝐤ei​𝐤⋅𝐑⟨un​𝐤|∇𝐤2|um​𝐤⟩.\langle{\bf R}n|r^{2}|{\bf 0}m\rangle=-{\frac{V}{(2\pi)^{3}}}\int d{\bf k}\,e^{i{\bf k}\cdot{\bf R}}\langle u_{n{\bf k}}|\nabla_{\bf k}^{2}|u_{m{\bf k}}\rangle\;\;. (24)

These expressions provide the needed connection with our underlying Bloch formalism, since they allow to express the localization functional Ω\Omega in terms of the matrix elements of ∇𝐤\nabla_{\bf k} and ∇𝐤2\nabla_{\bf k}^{2}. In addition, they allow to calculate the effects on the localization of any unitary transformation of the |un​𝐤⟩|u_{n{\bf k}}\rangle without having to recalculate expensive (especially when plane-wave basis sets are used) scalar products. We thus determine the Bloch orbitals |um​𝐤⟩|u_{m{\bf k}}\rangle on a regular mesh of k-points, and use finite differences to evaluate the above derivatives. In particular, we make the assumption that the BZ has been discretized into a uniform Monkhorst-Pack mesh, and the Bloch orbitals have been determined on that mesh.44 4 Even the case of Γ\Gamma-sampling – where the Brillouin zone is sampled with a single k-point – is encompassed by the above formulation. In this case the neighboring k-points are given by reciprocal lattice vectors 𝐆{\bf G} and the Bloch orbitals differ only by phase factors exp⁡(i​𝐆⋅𝐫)\exp(i{\bf G\cdot r}) from their counterparts at Γ\Gamma. The algebra does become simpler, though, as will be discussed in Sec. II.6.2.

For any f⁡(𝐤)f(\bf k) that is a smooth function of 𝐤\bf k, it can be shown that its gradient can be expressed by finite differences as

∇f​(𝐤)=∑𝐛wb​𝐛​[f⁡(𝐤+𝐛)−f⁡(𝐤)]+𝒪⁡(b2)\nabla f({\bf k})=\sum_{\bf b}\,w_{b}\,{\bf b}\,[f({\bf k+b})-f({\bf k})]+{\cal O}(b^{2})\;\; (25)

calculated on stars (“shells”) of near-neighbor k-points; here 𝐛\bf b is a vector connecting a 𝐤{\bf k}-point to one of its neighbors, wbw_{b} is an appropriate geometric factor that depends on the number of points in the star and its geometry (see Appendix B in Marzari and Vanderbilt [273] and Mostofi et al. [293] for a detailed description). In a similar way,

|∇f​(𝐤)|2=∑𝐛wb​[f⁡(𝐤+𝐛)−f⁡(𝐤)]2+𝒪⁡(b3).|\nabla f({\bf k})|^{2}=\sum_{\bf b}\,w_{b}\,[f({\bf k+b})-f({\bf k})]^{2}+{\cal O}(b^{3})\;\;. (26)

It now becomes straightforward to calculate the matrix elements in Eqs. (23) and (24). All the information needed for the reciprocal-space derivatives is encoded in the overlaps between Bloch orbitals at neighboring k-points

Mm​n(𝐤,𝐛)=⟨um​𝐤|un,𝐤+𝐛⟩.M_{mn}^{(\bf k,b)}=\langle u_{m\bf k}|u_{n,\bf k+b}\rangle\;\;. (27)

These overlaps play a central role in the formalism, since all contributions to the localization functional can be expressed in terms of them. Thus, once the Mm​n(𝐤,𝐛)M_{mn}^{(\bf k,b)} have been calculated, no further interaction with the electronic-structure code that calculated the ground state wavefunctions is necessary - making the entire Wannierization procedure a code-independent post-processing step 55 5 In particular, see Ferretti et al. [122] for the extension to ultrasoft pseudopotentials and the projector-augmented wave method, and Posternak et al. [342], Freimuth et al. [137], Kuneš et al. [234] for the full-potential linearized augmented planewave method.. There is no unique form for the localization functional in terms of the overlap elements, as it is possible to write down many alternative finite-difference expressions for 𝐫¯n\bar{\bf r}_{n} and ⟨r2⟩n\langle r^{2}\rangle_{n} which agree numerically to leading order in the mesh spacing bb (first and second order for 𝐫¯n\bar{\bf r}_{n} and ⟨r2⟩n\langle r^{2}\rangle_{n} respectively). We give here the expressions of Marzari and Vanderbilt [273], which have the desirable property of transforming correctly under gauge transformations that shift |𝟎​n⟩|{{\bf 0}n}\rangle by a lattice vector. They are

𝐫¯n=−1N∑𝐤,𝐛wb𝐛ImlnMn​n(𝐤,𝐛)\bar{\bf r}_{n}=-{\frac{1}{N}}\sum_{\bf k,b}\,w_{b}\,{\bf b}\,{\rm Im}\,\ln M_{nn}^{(\bf k,b)} (28)

(where we use, as outlined in Sec. II.1.3, the convention of Eq. (14)), and

⟨r2⟩n=1N​∑𝐤,𝐛wb​{[1−|Mn​n(𝐤,𝐛)|2]+[Im​ln⁡Mn​n(𝐤,𝐛)]2}.\langle r^{2}\rangle_{n}={\frac{1}{N}}\sum_{\bf k,b}\,w_{b}\,\left\{\left[1-|M_{nn}^{(\bf k,b)}|^{2}\right]+\left[{\rm Im}\,\ln M_{nn}^{(\bf k,b)}\right]^{2}\right\}\;\;. (29)

The corresponding expressions for the gauge-invariant and gauge-dependent parts of the spread functional are

ΩI=1N​∑𝐤,𝐛wb​(J−∑m​n|Mm​n(𝐤,𝐛)|2)\Omega_{\rm I}={\frac{1}{N}}\sum_{\bf k,b}\,w_{b}\,\Big(J-\sum_{mn}|M_{mn}^{(\bf k,b)}|^{2}\Big) (30)

and

Ω~\displaystyle\widetilde{\Omega} =\displaystyle= 1N​∑𝐤,𝐛wb​∑m≠n|Mm​n(𝐤,𝐛)|2\displaystyle\frac{1}{N}\sum_{\bf k,b}w_{b}\sum_{m\neq n}|M_{mn}^{\bf(k,b)}|^{2} (31)
+\displaystyle+ 1N​∑𝐤,𝐛wb​∑n(−Im​ln⁡Mn​n(𝐤,𝐛)−𝐛⋅𝐫¯n)2.\displaystyle{\frac{1}{N}}\sum_{\bf k,b}w_{b}\sum_{n}\left(-{\rm Im}\,\ln M_{nn}^{\bf(k,b)}-{\bf b}\cdot\bar{\bf r}_{n}\right)^{2}\;\;.

As mentioned, it is possible to write down alternative discretized expressions which agree numerically with Eqs. (28)–(31) up to the orders indicated in the mesh spacing bb; at the same time, one needs to be careful in realizing that certain quantities, such as the spreads, will display slow convergence with respect to the BZ sampling (see II.6.2 for a discussion), or that some exact results (e.g., that the sum of the centers of the Wannier functions is invariant with respect to unitary transformations) might acquire some numerical noise. In particular, Stengel and Spaldin [434] showed how to modify the above expressions in a way that renders the spread functional strictly invariant under BZ folding.

II.4 Localization procedure

In order to minimize the localization functional, we consider the first-order change of the spread functional Ω\Omega arising from an infinitesimal gauge transformation Um​n(𝐤)=δm​n+d​Wm​n(𝐤),U_{mn}^{\bf(k)}=\delta_{mn}+dW_{mn}^{\bf(k)}\,, where d​WdW is an infinitesimal anti-Hermitian matrix, d​W†=−d​WdW^{\dagger}=-dW, so that |un​𝐤⟩→|un​𝐤⟩+∑md​Wm​n(𝐤)​|um​𝐤⟩.|u_{n\bf k}\rangle\;\rightarrow\;|u_{n\bf k}\rangle+\sum_{m}dW_{mn}^{\bf(k)}\,|u_{m\bf k}\rangle\;. We use the convention

(d​Ωd​W)n​m=d​Ωd​Wm​n\left({\frac{d\Omega}{dW}}\right)_{nm}={\frac{d\Omega}{dW_{mn}}} (32)

(note the reversal of indices) and introduce 𝒜\cal A and 𝒮\cal S as the superoperators 𝒜⁡[B]=(B−B†)/2{\cal A}[B]=(B-B^{\dagger})/2 and 𝒮⁡[B]=(B+B†)/2​i{\cal S}[B]=(B+B^{\dagger})/2i. Defining

qn(𝐤,𝐛)=Im​ln⁡Mn​n(𝐤,𝐛)+𝐛⋅𝐫¯n,q_{n}^{\bf(k,b)}={\rm Im}\,\ln M_{nn}^{\bf(k,b)}+{\bf b\cdot\bar{r}}_{n}\,, (33)
Rm​n(𝐤,𝐛)=Mm​n(𝐤,𝐛)Mn​n(𝐤,𝐛)∗,R_{mn}^{\bf(k,b)}=M_{mn}^{\bf(k,b)}M_{nn}^{\bf(k,b)*}\,, (34)
Tm​n(𝐤,𝐛)=Mm​n(𝐤,𝐛)Mn​n(𝐤,𝐛)​qn(𝐤,𝐛),T_{mn}^{\bf(k,b)}=\frac{M_{mn}^{\bf(k,b)}}{M_{nn}^{\bf(k,b)}}\;q_{n}^{\bf(k,b)}\,, (35)

and referring to Marzari and Vanderbilt [273] for the details, we arrive at the explicit expression for the gradient G(𝐤)=d​Ω/d​W(𝐤)G^{\bf(k)}=d\Omega/dW^{\bf(k)} of the spread functional Ω\Omega as

G(𝐤)=4​∑𝐛wb​(𝒜⁡[R(𝐤,𝐛)]−𝒮⁡[T(𝐤,𝐛)]).G^{\bf(k)}=4\sum_{\bf b}\,w_{b}\left({\cal A}[R^{\bf(k,b)}]-{\cal S}[T^{\bf(k,b)}]\right)\;\;. (36)

This gradient is used to drive the evolution of the Um​n(𝐤)U_{mn}^{({\bf k})} (and, implicitly, of the |𝐑​n⟩|\,{{\bf R}n}\,\rangle of Eq. (10)) towards the minimum of Ω\Omega. A simple steepest-descent implementation, for example, takes small finite steps in the direction opposite to the gradient GG until a minimum is reached.

For details of the minimization strategies and the enforcement of unitarity during the search, the reader is referred to Mostofi et al. [293]. We should like to point out here, however, that most of the operations can be performed using inexpensive matrix algebra on small matrices. The most computationally demanding parts of the procedure are typically the calculation of the self-consistent Bloch orbitals |un​𝐤(0)⟩|u_{n\bf k}^{(0)}\rangle in the first place, and then the computation of a set of overlap matrices

Mm​n(0)​(𝐤,𝐛)=⟨um​𝐤(0)|un,𝐤+𝐛(0)⟩M_{mn}^{(0)\bf(k,b)}=\langle u_{m\bf k}^{(0)}|u_{n,\bf k+b}^{(0)}\rangle (37)

that are constructed once and for all from the |un​𝐤(0)⟩|u_{n\bf k}^{(0)}\rangle. After every update of the unitary matrices U(𝐤)U^{\bf(k)}, the overlap matrices are updated with inexpensive matrix algebra

M(𝐤,𝐛)=U(𝐤)†M(0)​(𝐤,𝐛)U(𝐤+𝐛)M^{\bf(k,b)}=U^{\bf(k)\dagger}\,M^{(0)\bf(k,b)}\,U^{\bf(k+b)} (38)

without any need to access the Bloch wavefunctions themselves. This not only makes the algorithm computationally fast and efficient, but also makes it independent of the basis used to represent the Bloch functions. That is, any electronic-structure code package capable of providing the set of overlap matrices M(𝐤,𝐛)M^{\bf(k,b)} can easily be interfaced to a common Wannier maximal-localization code.

II.5 Local minima

It should be noted that the localization functional can display, in addition to the desired global minimum, multiple local minima that do not lead to the construction of meaningful localized orbitals. Heuristically, it is also found that the WFs corresponding to these local minima are intrinsically complex, while they are found to be real, a part from a single complex phase, at the desired global minimum (provided of course that the calculations do not include spin-orbit coupling). Such observation in itself provides a useful diagnostic tool to weed out undesired solutions.

These false minima either correspond to the formation of topological defects (e.g., “vortices”) in an otherwise smooth gauge field in discrete 𝐤{\bf k} space, or they can arise when the branch cuts for the complex logarithms in Eq. (28) and Eq. (29) are inconsistent, i.e., when at any given k-point the contributions from different b-vectors differ by random amounts of 2π\pi in the logarithm. Since a locally appropriate choice of branch cuts can always be performed, this problem is less severe than the topological problem. The most straightforward way to avoid local minima altogether is to initialize the minimization procedure with a gauge choice that is already fairly smooth. For this purpose, the projection method already described in Sec. II.2 has been found to be extremely effective. Therefore, minimization is usually preceded by a projection step, to generate a set of analytic Bloch orbitals to be further optimized, as discussed more fully in Marzari and Vanderbilt [273] and Mostofi et al. [293].

II.6 The limit of isolated systems or large supercells

The formulation introduced above can be significantly simplified in two important and related cases, which merit a separate discussion. The first is the case of open boundary conditions: this is the most appropriate choice for treating finite, isolated systems (e.g., molecules and clusters) using localized basis sets, and is a common approach in quantum chemistry. The localization procedure can then be entirely recast in real space, and corresponds exactly to determining Foster-Boys localized orbitals. The second is the case of systems that can be described using very large periodic supercells. This is the most appropriate strategy for non-periodic bulk systems, such as amorphous solids or liquids (see Fig. 4 for a paradigmatic example), but obviously includes also periodic systems with large unit cells. In this approach, the Brillouin zone is considered to be sufficiently small that integrations over 𝐤{\bf k}-vectors can be approximated with a single 𝐤{\bf k}-point (usually at the Γ\Gamma point, i.e., the origin in reciprocal space). The localization procedure in this second case is based on the procedure for periodic boundary conditions described above, but with some notable simplifications. Isolated systems can also be artificially repeated and treated using the supercell approach, although care may be needed in dealing with the long-range electrostatics if the isolated entities are charged or have significant dipole or multipolar character [265, 92].

II.6.1 Real-space formulation for isolated systems

For an isolated system, described with open boundary conditions, all orbitals are localized to begin with, and further localization is achieved via unitary transformations within this set. We adopt a simplified notation |𝐑​n⟩→|wi⟩|{\bf R}n\rangle\rightarrow|w_{i}\rangle to refer to the localized orbitals of the isolated system that will become maximally localized. We decompose again the localization functional Ω=∑i[⟨r2⟩i−𝐫¯i2]\Omega=\sum_{i}[\langle r^{2}\rangle_{i}-\bar{\bf r}_{i}^{2}] into a term ΩI=∑αtr⁡[P​rα​Q​rα]\Omega_{\rm I}=\sum_{\alpha}{\rm tr}\,[Pr_{\alpha}Qr_{\alpha}] (where P=∑i|wi⟩​⟨wi|P=\sum_{i}|w_{i}\rangle\langle w_{i}|, Q=𝟏−PQ={\bf 1}-P, and ‘tr\rm tr’ refers to a sum over all the states wiw_{i}) that is invariant under unitary rotations, and a remainder Ω~=∑α∑i≠j|⟨wi|rα|wj⟩|2\widetilde{\Omega}=\sum_{\alpha}\sum_{i\neq j}\,|\langle w_{i}|r_{\alpha}|w_{j}\rangle|^{2} that needs to be minimized. Defining the matrices Xi​j=⟨wi|x|wj⟩X_{ij}=\langle w_{i}|x|w_{j}\rangle, XD,i​j=Xi​j​δi​jX_{{\rm D},ij}=X_{ij}\,\delta_{ij}, X′=X−XDX^{\prime}=X-X_{\rm D} (and similarly for YY and ZZ), Ω~\widetilde{\Omega} can be rewritten as

Ω~=tr⁡[X′ 2+Y′ 2+Z′ 2].\widetilde{\Omega}={\rm tr}\,[X^{\prime\,2}+Y^{\prime\,2}+Z^{\prime\,2}]\;\;. (39)

If XX, YY, and ZZ could be simultaneously diagonalized, then Ω~\widetilde{\Omega} would be minimized to zero (leaving only the invariant part). This is straightforward in one dimension, but is not generally possible in higher dimensions. The general solution to the three-dimensional problem consists instead in the optimal, but approximate, simultaneous co-diagonalization of the three Hermitian matrices XX, YY, and ZZ by a single unitary transformation that minimizes the numerical value of the localization functional. Although a formal solution to this problem is missing, implementing a numerical procedure (e.g., by steepest-descent or conjugate-gradients minimization) is fairly straightforward. It should be noted that the problem of simultaneous co-diagonalization arises also in the context of multivariate analysis [129] and signal processing [71], and has been recently revisited in relation with the present localization approach [164] (see also Sec. IIIA in Berghold et al. [32]).

To proceed further, we write

d​Ω=2​tr​[X′​d​X+Y′​d​Y+Z′​d​Z],d\Omega=2\,{\rm tr}\,[X^{\prime}dX+Y^{\prime}dY+Z^{\prime}dZ]\;\;, (40)

exploiting the fact that tr⁡[X′​XD]=0{\rm tr}\,[X^{\prime}X_{\rm D}]=0, and similarly for YY and ZZ. We then consider an infinitesimal unitary transformation |wi⟩→|wi⟩+∑jd​Wj​i​|wj⟩|w_{i}\rangle\;\rightarrow\;|w_{i}\rangle+\sum_{j}dW_{ji}|w_{j}\rangle (where d​WdW is antihermitian), from which d​X=[X,d​W]dX=[X,dW], and similarly for YY, ZZ. Inserting in Eq. (40) and using tr⁡[A⁡[B,C]]=tr⁡[C⁡[A,B]]{\rm tr}\,[A[B,C]]=\,{\rm tr}\,[C[A,B]] and [X′,X]=[X′,XD][X^{\prime},X]=[X^{\prime},X_{\rm D}], we obtain d​Ω=tr⁡[d​W​G]d\Omega={\rm tr}\,[dW\,G] where the gradient of the spread functional G=d​Ω/d​WG={d\Omega/dW} is given by

G=2​{[X′,XD]+[Y′,YD]+[Z′,ZD]​d​W}.G=2\,\Bigl\{[X^{\prime},X_{\rm D}]+[Y^{\prime},Y_{\rm D}]+[Z^{\prime},Z_{\rm D}]\,dW\Bigr\}\;\;. (41)

The minimization can then be carried out using a procedure similar to that outlined above for periodic boundary conditions. Last, we note that minimizing Ω~\widetilde{\Omega} is equivalent to maximizing tr⁡[XD2+YD2+ZD2]{\rm tr}\,[X^{2}_{\rm D}+Y^{2}_{\rm D}+Z^{2}_{\rm D}], since tr⁡[X′​XD]=tr⁡[Y′​YD]=tr⁡[Y′​YD]=0{\rm tr}\,[X^{\prime}X_{\rm D}]={\rm tr}\,[Y^{\prime}Y_{\rm D}]={\rm tr}\,[Y^{\prime}Y_{\rm D}]=0.

II.6.2 Γ\Gamma-point formulation for large supercells

A similar formulation applies in reciprocal space when dealing with isolated or very large systems in periodic boundary conditions, i.e., whenever it becomes appropriate to sample the wavefunctions only at the Γ\Gamma-point of the Brillouin zone. For simplicity, we start with the case of a simple cubic lattice of spacing LL, and define the matrices 𝒳\cal{X}, 𝒴\cal{Y}, and 𝒵\cal{Z} as

𝒳m​n=⟨wm|e−2πix/L|wn⟩{\cal{X}}_{mn}=\langle w_{m}|e^{-2\pi ix/L}|w_{n}\rangle (42)

and its periodic permutations (the extension to supercells of arbitrary symmetry has been derived by Silvestrelli [404]).66 6 We point out that the definition of the 𝒳,𝒴,𝒵\cal{X},\cal{Y},\cal{Z} matrices for extended systems, now common in the literature, is different from the one used in the previous subsection for the X,Y,ZX,Y,Z matrices for isolated system. We preserved these two notations for the sake of consistency with published work, at the cost of making less evident the close similarities that exist between the two minimization algorithms. The coordinate xnx_{n} of the nn-th WF center (WFC) can then be obtained from

xn=−L2​π​Im​ln​⟨wn|e−i​2​πL​x|wn⟩=−L2​π​Im​ln​𝒳n​n,x_{n}=-{\frac{L}{{2\pi}}}\,{\rm Im}\;{\rm ln}\langle w_{n}|e^{-i{\frac{2\pi}{L}}x}|w_{n}\rangle=-{\frac{L}{{2\pi}}}\,{\rm Im}\;{\rm ln}\;{\cal{X}}_{nn}\;, (43)

and similarly for yny_{n} and znz_{n}. Equation (43) has been shown by Resta [357] to be the correct definition of the expectation value of the position operator for a system with periodic boundary conditions, and had been introduced several years ago to deal with the problem of determining the average position of a single electronic orbital in a periodic supercell [392] (the above definition becomes self-evident in the limit where wnw_{n} tends to a Dirac delta function).

Following the derivation of the previous subsection, or of Silvestrelli et al. [410], it can be shown that the maximum-localization criterion is equivalent to maximizing the functional

Ξ=∑n=1J(|𝒳n​n|2+|𝒴n​n|2+|𝒵n​n|2).\Xi=\sum_{n=1}^{J}\left(|{\cal{X}}_{nn}|^{2}+|{\cal{Y}}_{nn}|^{2}+|{\cal{Z}}_{nn}|^{2}\right)\;. (44)

The first term of the gradient d​Ξ/d​Am​nd\Xi/dA_{mn} is given by [𝒳n​m​(𝒳n​n∗−𝒳m​m∗)−𝒳m​n∗​(𝒳m​m−𝒳n​n)][{\cal{X}}_{nm}({\cal{X}}_{nn}^{*}-{\cal{X}}_{mm}^{*})-{\cal{X}}_{mn}^{*}({\cal{X}}_{mm}-{\cal{X}}_{nn})], and similarly for the second and third terms. Again, once the gradient is determined, minimization can be performed using a steepest-descent or conjugate-gradients algorithm; as always, the computational cost of the localization procedure is small, given that it involves only small matrices of dimension J×JJ\times J, once the scalar products needed to construct the initial 𝒳(0){\cal{X}}^{(0)}, 𝒴(0){\cal{Y}}^{(0)} and 𝒵(0){\cal{Z}}^{(0)} have been calculated, which takes an effort of order J2∗NbasisJ^{2}*N_{\rm basis}. We note that in the limit of a single 𝐤{\bf k} point the distinction between Bloch orbitals and WFs becomes irrelevant, since no Fourier transform from 𝐤{\bf k} to 𝐑{\bf R} is involved in the transformation Eq. (10); rather, we want to find the optimal unitary matrix that rotates the ground-state self-consistent orbitals into their maximally localized representation, making this problem exactly equivalent to the one of isolated systems. Interestingly, it should also be mentioned that the local minima alluded to in the previous subsection are typically not found when using Γ\Gamma sampling in large supercells.

Before concluding, we note that care should be taken when comparing the spreads of MLWFs calculated in supercells of different sizes. The Wannier centers and the general shape of the MLWFs often converge rapidly as the cell size is increased, but even for the ideal case of an isolated molecule, the total spread Ω\Omega often displays much slower convergence. This behavior derives from the finite-difference representation of the invariant part ΩI\Omega_{\,\rm I} of the localization functional (essentially, a second derivative); while ΩI\Omega_{\,\rm I} does not enter into the localization procedure, it does contribute to the spread, and in fact usually represents the largest term. This slow convergence was noted by Marzari and Vanderbilt [273] when commenting on the convergence properties of Ω\Omega with respect to the spacing of the Monkhorst-Pack mesh, and has been studied in detail by others [475, 434]. For isolated systems in a supercell, this problem can be avoided simply by using a very large LL in Eq. (43), since in practice the integrals only need to be calculated in the small region where the orbitals are non-zero [499]. For extended bulk systems, this convergence problem can be ameliorated significantly by calculating the position operator using real-space integrals [246, 434, 244].

II.7 Exponential localization

The existence of exponentially localized WFs – i.e., WFs whose tails decay exponentially fast – is a famous problem in the band theory of solids, with close ties to the general properties of the insulating state [213]. While the asymptotic decay of a Fourier transform can be related to the analyticity of the function and its derivatives (see, e.g., Duffin [101], Duffin and Shaffer [102] and references therein), proofs of exponential localization for the Wannier transform were obtained over the years only for limited cases, starting with the work of Kohn [212], who considered a one-dimensional crystal with inversion symmetry. Other milestones include the work of des Cloizeaux [81], who established the exponential localization in 1D crystals without inversion symmetry and in the centrosymmetric 3D case, and the subsequent removal of the requirement of inversion symmetry in the latter case by Nenciu [302]. The asymptotic behavior of WFs was further clarified by He and Vanderbilt [172], who found that the exponential decay is modulated by a power law. In dimensions d>1d>1 the problem is further complicated by the possible existence of band degeneracies, while the proofs of des Cloizeaux and Nenciu were restricted to isolated bands. The early work on composite bands in 3D only established the exponential localization of the projection operator PP, Eq. (13), not of the WFs themselves [80].

The question of exponential decay in 2D and 3D was finally settled by Brouder et al. [58] who showed, as a corollary to a theorem by Panati [323], that a necessary and sufficient condition for the existence of exponentially localized WFs in 2D and 3D is that the so-called “Chern invariants” for the composite set of bands vanish identically. Panati [323] had demonstrated that this condition ensures the possibility of carrying out the gauge transformation of Eq. (8) in such a way that the resulting cell-periodic states |u~n​𝐤⟩|{\tilde{u}_{n{\bf k}}}\rangle are analytic functions of 𝐤{\bf k} across the entire BZ;77 7 Conversely, nonzero Chern numbers pose an obstruction to finding a globally smooth gauge in 𝐤{\bf k}-space. The mathematical definition of a Chern number is given in Sec. V.3.4. this in turn implies the exponential falloff of the WFs given by Eq. (10).

It is natural to ask whether the MLWFs obtained by minimizing the quadratic spread functional Ω\Omega are also exponentially localized. Marzari and Vanderbilt [273] established this in 1D, by simply noting that the MLWF construction then reduces to finding the eigenstates of the projected position operator P​x​PPxP, a case for which exponential localization had already been proven [305]. The more complex problem of exponential localization of MLWFs for composite bands in 2D and 3D was finally proven by Panati and Pisante [324].

II.8 Hybrid Wannier functions

It is sometimes useful to carry out the Wannier transform in one spatial dimension only, leaving wavefunctions that are still delocalized and Bloch-periodic in the remaining directions [393]. Such orbitals are usually denoted as “hermaphrodite” or “hybrid” WFs. Explicitly, Eq. (10) is replaced by the hybrid WF definition

|l,n𝐤∥⟩=c2​π∫02​π/c|ψn​𝐤⟩e−i​l​k⟂​cdk⟂,|\,{l,n{\bf k}_{\parallel}}\,\rangle\;=\;\frac{c}{2\pi}\;\int_{0}^{2\pi/c}|{\,\psi_{n{\bf k}}\,}\rangle\,e^{-ilk_{\perp}c}\,dk_{\perp}\;, (45)

where 𝐤∥{\bf k}_{\parallel} is the wavevector in the plane (delocalized directions) and k⟂k_{\perp}, ll, and cc are the wavevector, cell index, and cell dimension in the direction of localization. The 1D Wannier construction can be done independently for each 𝐤∥{\bf k}_{\parallel} using direct (i.e., non-iterative) methods as described in Sec. IV C 1 of Marzari and Vanderbilt [273].

Such a construction has proved useful for a variety of purposes, from verifying numerically exponential localization in 1 dimension, to treating electric polarization or applied electric fields along a specific spatial direction [154, 152, 497, 434, 296] or for analyzing aspects of topological insulators [84, 424, 423]. Examples will be discussed in Secs. V.2.2 and VI.1.4.

II.9 Entangled bands

The methods described in the previous sections were designed with isolated groups of bands in mind, separated from all other bands by finite gaps throughout the entire Brillouin zone. However, in many applications the bands of interest are not isolated. This can happen, for example, when studying electron transport, which is governed by the partially filled bands close to the Fermi level, or when dealing with empty bands, such as the four low-lying antibonding bands of tetrahedral semiconductors, which are attached to higher conduction bands. Another case of interest is when a partially filled manifold is to be downfolded into a basis of WFs - e.g., to construct model Hamiltonians. In all these examples the desired bands lie within a limited energy range but overlap and hybridize with other bands which extend further out in energy. We will refer to them as entangled bands.

The difficulty in treating entangled bands stems from the fact that it is unclear exactly which states to choose to form JJ WFs, particularly in those regions of 𝐤{\bf k}-space where the bands of interest are hybridized with other unwanted bands. Before a Wannier localization procedure can be applied, some prescription is needed for constructing JJ states per 𝐤{\bf k}-point from a linear combination of the states in this larger manifold. Once a suitable JJ-dimensional Bloch manifold has been identified at each 𝐤{\bf k}, the same procedure described earlier for an isolated group of bands can be used to generate localized WFs spanning that manifold.

The problem of computing well localized WFs starting from entangled bands is thus broken down into two distinct steps, subspace selection and gauge selection. As we will see, the same guiding principle can be used for both steps, namely, to achieve “smoothness” in 𝐤{\bf k}-space. In the subspace selection step a JJ-dimensional Bloch manifold which varies smoothly as function of 𝐤{\bf k} is constructed. In the gauge-selection step that subspace is represented using a set of JJ Bloch functions which are themselves smooth functions of 𝐤{\bf k}, such that the corresponding WFs are well localized.

II.9.1 Subspace selection via projection

The projection technique discussed in Section II.2 can be easily adapted to produce JJ smoothly-varying Bloch-like states starting from a larger set of Bloch bands [426]. The latter can be chosen, for example, as the bands lying within a given energy window, or within a specified range of band indices. Their number 𝒥𝐤≥J{\cal J}_{\bf k}\geq J is not required to be constant throughout the BZ.

We start from a set of JJ localized trial orbitals gn​(𝐫)g_{n}(\bf r) and project each of them onto the space spanned by the chosen eigenstates at each 𝐤{\bf k},

|ϕn​𝐤⟩=∑m=1𝒥𝐤|ψm​𝐤⟩​⟨ψm​𝐤|gn⟩.|\phi_{n\bf k}\rangle=\sum_{m=1}^{{\cal J}_{\bf k}}\,|\psi_{m\bf k}\rangle\,\langle\psi_{m\bf k}|g_{n}\rangle\;. (46)

This is identical to Eq. (16), except for the fact that the overlap matrix (A𝐤)m​n=⟨ψm​𝐤|gn⟩(A_{\bf k})_{mn}=\langle\psi_{m\bf k}|g_{n}\rangle has become rectangular with dimensions 𝒥𝐤×J{\cal J}_{\bf k}\times J. We then orthonormalize the resulting JJ orbitals using Eq. (17), to produce a set of JJ smoothly-varying Bloch-like states across the BZ,

|ψ~n​𝐤⟩=∑m=1J|ϕm​𝐤⟩(S𝐤−1/2)m​n.|\tilde{\psi}_{n\bf k}\rangle=\sum_{m=1}^{J}\,|\phi_{m\bf k}\rangle(S_{\bf k}^{-1/2})_{mn}\;. (47)

As in Eq. (17), (S𝐤)m​n=⟨ϕm​𝐤|ϕn​𝐤⟩V=(A𝐤†​A𝐤)m​n(S_{\bf k})_{mn}={\langle\phi_{m\bf k}|\phi_{n\bf k}\rangle_{V}}=(A_{\bf k}^{\dagger}A_{\bf k}^{\phantom{\dagger}})_{mn}, but with rectangular A𝐤A_{\bf k} matrices.

The above procedure achieves simultaneously the two goals of subspace selection and gauge selection, although neither of them is performed optimally. The gauge selection can be further refined by minimizing Ω~\widetilde{\Omega} within the projected subspace. It is also possible to refine iteratively the subspace selection itself, as will be described in the next section. However, for many applications this one-shot procedure is perfectly adequate, and in some cases it may even be preferable to more sophisticated iterative approaches (see also Sec. III.3.) For example, it often results in “symmetry-adapted” WFs which inherit the symmetry properties of the trial orbitals [228].

As an example, we plot in Fig. 5 the eight disentangled bands obtained by projecting the band structure of silicon, taken within an energy window that coincides with the entire energy axis shown, onto eight atomic-like s​p3sp^{3} hybrids. The disentangled bands, generated using Wannier interpolation (Sec. VI.1), are shown as blue triangles, along with the original first-principles bands (solid lines). While the overall agreement is quite good, significant deviations can be seen wherever higher unoccupied and unwanted states possessing some significant s​p3sp^{3} character are admixed into the projected manifold. This behavior can be avoided by forcing certain Bloch states to be preserved identically in the projected manifold - we refer to those as belonging to a frozen “inner” window, since this is often the simplest procedure for selecting them. The placement and range of this inner window will depend on the problem at hand. For example, in order to describe the low-energy physics for, e.g., transport calculations, the inner window would typically include all states in a desired range around the Fermi level.

We show as red circles in Fig. 5 the results obtained by forcing the entire valence manifold to be preserved, leading to a set of eight projected bands that reproduce exactly the four valence bands, and follow quite closely the four low-lying conduction bands. For the modifications to the projection algorithm required to enforce this frozen inner window, we refer to Sec. III.G of Souza et al. [426].

Projection techniques can work very well, and an application of this approach to graphene is shown in Fig. 6, where the π/π⋆\pi/\pi^{\star} manifold is disentangled with great accuracy by a simple projection onto atomic pzp_{z} orbitals, or the entire occupied manifold together with π/π⋆\pi/\pi^{\star} manifold is obtained by projection onto atomic pzp_{z} and s​p2sp^{2} orbitals (one every other atom, for the case of the s​p2sp^{2} orbitals - albeit bond-centered ss orbitals would work equally well).

Projection methods have been extensively used to study strongly-correlated systems [228, 16, 33], in particular to identify a “correlated subspace” for LDA+U or DMFT calculations, as will be discussed in more detail in Sec. VII. It has also been argued [227] that projected WFs provide a more appropriate basis for the study of defects, as the pursuit of better localization in a MLWF scheme risks defining the gauge differently for the defect WF as compared to the bulk. Instead, a straightforward projection approach ensures the similarity between the WF in the defect (supercell) and in the pristine (primitive cell) calculations, and this has been exploited to develop a scheme to unfold the band-structure of disordered supercells into the Brillouin zone of the underlying primitive cell, allowing a direct comparison with angular resolved photoemission spectroscopy experiments [227].

II.9.2 Subspace selection via optimal smoothness

The projection onto trial orbitals provides a simple and effective way of extracting a smooth Bloch subspace starting from a larger set of entangled bands. The reason for its success is easily understood: the localization of the trial orbitals in real space leads to smoothness in 𝐤{\bf k}-space. In order to further refine the subspace selection procedure, it is useful to introduce a precise measure of the smoothness in 𝐤{\bf k}-space of a manifold of Bloch states. The search for an optimally-smooth subspace can then be formulated as a minimization problem, similar to the search for an optimally-smooth gauge.

As it turns out, smoothness in 𝐤{\bf k} of a Bloch space is precisely what is measured by the functional ΩI\Omega_{\rm I} introduced in Sec. II.3.1. We know from Eq. (19) that the quadratic spread Ω\Omega of the WFs spanning a Bloch space of dimension JJ comprises two positive-definite contributions, one gauge-invariant (ΩI\Omega_{\rm I}), the other gauge-dependent (Ω~\widetilde{\Omega}). Given such a Bloch space (e.g., an isolated group of bands, or a group of bands previously disentangled via projection), we have seen that the optimally smooth gauge can be found by minimizing Ω~\widetilde{\Omega} with respect to the unitary mixing of states within that space.

From this perspective, the gauge-invariance of ΩI\Omega_{\rm I} means that this quantity is insensitive to the smoothness of the individual Bloch states |u~n​𝐤⟩|{\tilde{u}_{n{\bf k}}}\rangle chosen to represent the Hilbert space. But considering that ΩI\Omega_{\rm I} is a part of the spread functional, it must describe smoothness in some other sense. What ΩI\Omega_{\rm I} manages to capture is the intrinsic smoothness of the underlying Hilbert space. This can be seen starting from the discretized 𝐤{\bf k}-space expression for ΩI\Omega_{\rm I}, Eq. (30), and noting that it can be written as

ΩI=1N​∑𝐤,𝐛wb​T𝐤,𝐛\Omega_{\rm I}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{{\bf k},{\bf b}}\,w_{b}\,T_{{\bf k},{\bf b}} (48)

with

T𝐤,𝐛=Tr⁡[P𝐤​Q𝐤+𝐛],T_{{\bf k},{\bf b}}={\rm Tr}[{P}_{\bf k}\,{Q}_{{\bf k}+{\bf b}}], (49)

where P𝐤=∑n=1J|u~n​𝐤⟩​⟨u~n​𝐤|{P}_{\bf k}=\sum_{n=1}^{J}\,|{\tilde{u}_{n\bf k}}\rangle\langle\tilde{u}_{n\bf k}| is the gauge-invariant projector onto the Bloch subspace at 𝐤{\bf k}, Q𝐤=𝟏−P𝐤{Q}_{\bf k}={\bf 1}-{P}_{\bf k}, and “Tr” denotes the electronic trace over the full Hilbert space. It is now evident that T𝐤,𝐛T_{{\bf k},{\bf b}} measures the degree of mismatch (or “spillage”) between the neighboring Bloch subspaces at 𝐤{\bf k} and 𝐤+𝐛{\bf k}+{\bf b}, vanishing when they are identical, and that ΩI\Omega_{\rm I} provides a BZ average of the local subspace mismatch.

The optimized subspace selection procedure can now be formulated as follows [426]. A set of 𝒥𝐤≥J{\cal J}_{\bf k}\geq J Bloch states is identified at each point on a uniform BZ grid, using, for example, an energy window. An iterative procedure is then used to extract self-consistently across the BZ the JJ-dimensional subspaces having collectively the smallest possible value of ΩI\Omega_{\rm I} (typically the minimization starts from an initial guess for the target subspaces given, e.g., by projection onto trial orbitals). Viewed as function of 𝐤{\bf k}, the Bloch subspace obtained at the end of the minimization is “optimally smooth” in that it changes as little as possible with 𝐤{\bf k}. The minimization algorithm can be easily modified in order to preserve identically the Bloch eigenstates within an inner energy window.

As in the case of the one-shot projection, the outcome of this iterative procedure is a set of JJ Bloch-like states at each 𝐤{\bf k} which are linear combinations of the initial 𝒥𝐤{\cal J}_{\bf k} eigenstates. One important difference is that the resulting states are not guaranteed to be individually smooth, and the minimization of ΩI\Omega_{\rm I} must therefore be followed by a gauge-selection step, which is in every way identical to the one described earlier for isolated groups of bands. Alternatively, it is possible to combine the two steps, and minimize Ω=ΩI+Ω~\Omega=\Omega_{\rm I}+\widetilde{\Omega} simultaneously with respect to the choice of Hilbert subspace and the choice of gauge [459, 460]; this should lead to the most-localized set of JJ WFs that can be constructed from the initial 𝒥𝐤{\cal J}_{\bf k} Bloch states. In all three cases, the entire process amounts to a linear transformation taking from 𝒥𝐤{\cal J}_{\bf k} initial eigenstates to JJ smooth Bloch-like states,

|ψ~n​𝐤⟩=∑m=1𝒥𝐤|ψm​𝐤⟩​V𝐤,m​n.|{\tilde{\psi}_{n{\bf k}}}\rangle=\sum_{m=1}^{{\cal J}_{\bf k}}\,|{\psi_{m{\bf k}}}\rangle V_{{\bf k},mn}. (50)

In the case of the projection procedure, the explicit expression for the 𝒥𝐤×J{\cal J}_{{\bf k}}\times J matrix V𝐤V_{\bf k} can be surmised from Eqs. (46) and (47).

Let us compare the one-shot projection and iterative procedures for subspace selection, using crystalline copper as an example. Suppose we want to disentangle the five narrow dd bands from the wide ss band that crosses and hybridizes with them, to construct a set of well-localized dd-like WFs. The bands that result from projecting onto five dd-type atomic orbitals are shown as blue triangles in Fig. 7. They follow very closely the first-principles bands away from the ss-dd hybridization regions, where the interpolated bands remain narrow.

The red circles show the results obtained using the iterative scheme to extract an optimally-smooth five-dimensional manifold. The maximal “global smoothness of connection” is achieved by keeping the five dd-like states and excluding the ss-like state. This happens because the smoothness criterion embodied by Eqs. (48) and (49) implies that the orbital character is preserved as much as possible while traversing the BZ. Inspection of the resulting MLWFs confirms their atomic dd-like character. They are also significantly more localized than the ones obtained by projection and the corresponding disentangled bands are somewhat better behaved, displaying less spurious oscillations in the hybridization regions.

In addition, there are cases where the flexibility of the minimization algorithm leads to surprising optimal states whose symmetries would not have been self-evident in advance. One case is shown in Fig. 8. Here we wish to construct a minimal Wannier basis for copper, describing both the narrow dd-like bands and the wide free-electron-like band with which they hybridize. By choosing different dimensions for the disentangled subspace, it was found that the composite set of bands is faithfully represented by seven MLWFs, of which five are the standard dd-like orbitals, and the remaining two are ss-like orbitals centered at the tetrahedral interstitial sites of the fcc structure. The latter arise from the constructive interference between s​p3sp^{3} orbitals that would be part of the ideal s​p3​d5sp^{3}d^{5} basis set; in this case, bands up to 20 eV above the Fermi energy can be meaningfully described with a minimal basis set of seven orbitals, that would have been difficult to identify using only educated guesses for the projections.

The concept of a natural dimension for the disentangled manifold has been explored further by Thygesen et al. [459], Thygesen et al. [460]. As illustrated in Fig. 9, they showed that by minimizing Ω=ΩI+Ω~\Omega=\Omega_{\rm I}+\widetilde{\Omega} for different choices of JJ, one can find an optimal JJ such that the resulting “partially-occupied” Wannier functions are most localized (provided enough bands are used to capture the bonding and anti-bonding combinations of those atomic-like WFs).

II.9.3 Iterative minimization of ΩI\Omega_{\rm I}

The minimization of ΩI\Omega_{\rm I} inside an energy window is conveniently done using an algebraic algorithm [426]. The stationarity condition δ​ΩI​({u~n​𝐤})=0\delta\Omega_{\rm I}(\{\tilde{u}_{n\bf k}\})=0, subject to orthonormality constraints, is equivalent to solving the set of eigenvalue equations

[∑𝐛wbP𝐤+𝐛]|u~n​𝐤⟩=λn​𝐤|u~n​𝐤⟩.\Big[\sum_{\bf b}\,w_{b}\,{P}_{{\bf k}+{\bf b}}\Big]\left|\left.\tilde{u}_{n{\bf k}}\right\rangle\right.=\lambda_{n\bf k}\left|\left.\tilde{u}_{n{\bf k}}\right\rangle\right.. (51)

Clearly these equations, one for each 𝐤{\bf k}-point, are coupled, so that the problem has to be solved self-consistently throughout the Brillouin zone. This can be done using an iterative procedure: on the ii-th iteration go through all the 𝐤{\bf k}-points in the grid, and for each of them find JJ orthonormal states |u~n​𝐤(i)⟩\left|\left.\tilde{u}_{n\bf k}^{(i)}\right\rangle\right., defining a subspace whose spillage over the neighboring subspaces from the previous iteration is as small as possible. At each step the set of equations

[∑𝐛wbP𝐤+𝐛(i−1)]|u~n​𝐤(i)⟩=λn​𝐤(i)|u~n​𝐤(i)⟩\Big[\sum_{\bf b}\,w_{b}\,{P}_{{\bf k}+{\bf b}}^{(i-1)}\Big]\left|\left.\tilde{u}_{n{\bf k}}^{(i)}\right\rangle\right.=\lambda_{n\bf k}^{(i)}\left|\left.\tilde{u}_{n{\bf k}}^{(i)}\right\rangle\right. (52)

is solved, and the JJ eigenvectors with largest eigenvalues are selected. That choice ensures that at self-consistency the stationary point corresponds to the absolute minimum of ΩI\Omega_{\rm I}.

In practice Eq. (52) is solved in the basis of the original 𝒥𝐤{\cal J}_{\bf k} Bloch eigenstates |un​𝐤⟩|u_{n\bf k}\rangle inside the energy window. Each iteration then amounts to diagonalizing the following 𝒥𝐤×𝒥𝐤{\cal J}_{\bf k}\times{\cal J}_{\bf k} Hermitian matrix at every 𝐤{\bf k}:

Zm​n(i)​(𝐤)=⟨um​𝐤|∑𝐛wb​[P𝐤+𝐛(i−1)]in|un​𝐤⟩.Z_{mn}^{(i)}({\bf k})=\Big<u_{m\bf k}\Big|\sum_{\bf b}w_{b}{\left[{P}^{(i-1)}_{{\bf k}+{\bf b}}\right]}_{\rm in}\Big|u_{n\bf k}\Big>. (53)

Since these are small matrices, each step of the iterative procedure is computationally inexpensive.

As a final comment, we mention that in the case of degeneracies or quasi degeneracies in the spreads of orbitals centered on the same site, the localization algorithm will perform rather arbitrary mixing of these (as can be the case, e.g., for the dd or ff electrons of a transition-metal ion, or for its t2​gt_{2g} or ege_{g} groups). A solution to this problem is to diagonalize an operator with the desired symmetry in the basis of the Wannier functions that have been obtained (see Posternak et al. [342] for the example of the dd orbitals in MnO).

II.9.4 Localization and local minima

Empirical evidence and experience suggests that localized Wannier functions can be readily constructed also in the case of an entangled manifold of bands: Even for metals, smooth manifolds can be disentangled and “wannierized” to give MLWFs. Such disentangled MLWFs, e.g., the pzp_{z} MLWFs describing the π\pi/π∗\pi^{\ast} manifold of graphene shown in Fig. 6, are found to be strongly localized. While exponential localization has not been proven, both numerical evidence and the analogy with the isolated composite case suggest this might be the case.

Problems associated with reaching local minima of the spread functional, and with obtaining Wannier functions that are not real-valued, are more pronounced in the case of entangled bands. They are usually alleviated by careful reconsideration of the energy windows used, in order to include higher energy states of the appropriate symmetry, and/or by using a better initial guess for the projections. We infer, therefore, that such problems are associated not with the wannierization part of the procedure, but rather with the initial selection of the smooth subspace from the full manifold of entangled bands.

It is worth noting that the Γ\Gamma-point formulation (Sec. II.6.2) appears to be less affected by these problems. In cases where it is not intuitive or obvious what the MLWFs should be, therefore, it can often be a fruitful strategy to use the Γ\Gamma-point formulation to obtain approximate MLWFs that may then be used to inform the initial guess for a subsequent calculation with a full k-point mesh.

II.10 Many-body generalizations

The concept of WFs is closely tied to the framework of single-particle Hamiltonians. Only in this case can we define JJ occupied single-particle Bloch functions at each wavevector 𝐤{\bf k} and treat all JJ of them on an equal footing, allowing for invariance with respect to unitary mixing among them. Once the two-particle electron-electron interaction is formally included in the Hamiltonian, the many-body wavefunction cannot be reduced to any simple form allowing for the construction of WFs in the usual sense.

One approach is to consider the reduced one-particle density matrix

n⁡(𝐫,𝐫′)=∫Ψ∗​(𝐫,𝐫2​…)​Ψ​(𝐫′,𝐫2,…)​d​𝐫2​d​𝐫3​…n({\bf r},{\bf r}^{\prime})=\int\Psi^{*}({\bf r},{\bf r}_{2}...)\,\Psi({\bf r}^{\prime},{\bf r}_{2},...)\,d{\bf r}_{2}\,d{\bf r}_{3}... (54)

for a many-body insulator. Since n⁡(𝐫,𝐫′)n({\bf r},{\bf r}^{\prime}) is periodic in the sense of n⁡(𝐫+𝐑,𝐫′+𝐑)=n⁡(𝐫,𝐫′)n({\bf r}+{\bf R},{\bf r}^{\prime}+{\bf R})=n({\bf r},{\bf r}^{\prime}), its eigenvectors – the so-called “natural orbitals” – have the form of Bloch functions carrying a label n,𝐤n,{\bf k}.
